South African motor insurance guide

The app may protect a trip. It does not automatically insure the car that earns your income.

E-hailing insurance in South Africa starts with one clear fact: if you carry passengers for reward, your insurer must know. An ordinary private-use motor policy and a platform safety benefit solve different problems.

Quick answer Uber, Bolt and inDrive drivers should have motor cover that explicitly accepts carrying passengers for reward, plus the right licence and permit. Platform benefits are supplementary: for example, Uber says its AIG Partner Injury Protection applies while “On-Trip” but is not commercial vehicle insurance. Uber South Africa

E-hailing changes the risk your policy is covering

Carrying fare-paying passengers is commercial use, not a small extension of the school run or commute. The vehicle is on the road more often, may operate late at night, visits changing areas, carries members of the public and can be the driver's main income-producing asset.

That does not mean every private policy uses identical wording or that every e-hailing driver needs the same product. It means the use must be disclosed and accepted. “Comprehensive” tells you broadly which types of loss may be insured; it does not, by itself, tell you that Uber, Bolt or inDrive work is an allowed use.

The practical starting point is to compare the proposed wording with a sound car-insurance checklist and the actual work the car performs. A broker may help route a commercial risk, but the insurer's schedule and wording remain decisive.

Private, business and e-hailing use are not interchangeable
UseWhat it usually meansThe question that mattersMain gap to avoid
Private usePersonal, social and commuting use within the wording.Does the policy permit any paid passenger transport?Assuming comprehensive cover changes the permitted use.
Business useTravel for work, such as visiting clients, depending on the policy.Does “business” expressly include passengers for reward?Treating a business-use tick-box as taxi cover.
E-hailing useApp-based public transport using the insured vehicle.Which apps, drivers, trip stages and territories are accepted?Leaving the insurer unaware of platform work or multiple drivers.
Fleet or rental useOne or more vehicles used by hired, nominated or rotating drivers.Are ownership, finance and every driver arrangement declared?Insuring the owner but not the real driving structure.

This distinction is more than theory. In its 2024 annual report, the National Financial Ombud Scheme said motor vehicle insurance accounted for 42% of non-life complaints finalised that year. The report is not an e-hailing-only dataset, but it shows why usage, exclusions and claim conditions deserve careful attention. NFO Annual Report 2024

Platform protection is useful, but it is not your motor policy

Platform benefits can help with defined injuries or incidents during a ride, yet they should not be read as a promise to repair or replace the driver's car. Each platform publishes a different level of detail, and only the current terms issued by the platform or insurer are binding.

Uber: the clearest public boundary

Uber's South African page says Partner Injury Protection is accident insurance from AIG. It protects eligible drivers, delivery partners and riders from acceptance of a request until the trip or delivery ends, subject to terms and limits. Crucially, Uber also says the benefit does not provide commercial vehicle insurance and is not a substitute for comprehensive vehicle insurance. Uber Partner Injury Protection

Bolt: confirm the insurance document in-app

Bolt's public South African driver material clearly requires a valid PrDP and tells vehicle owners to apply for an operating licence. Its detailed operating-licence guide also explains the Form 1B and platform affiliation-letter process. Bolt driver requirements Bolt operating-licence guide

We did not find a current, public, South Africa-specific Bolt policy wording that clearly states when platform insurance starts, what it pays, its limits and whether the driver's own vehicle is covered. That is an evidence gap, not proof of no protection. Drivers should request the current wording through the Bolt Driver app or support and still arrange motor cover that expressly accepts e-hailing.

inDrive: a broad promise without public detail

inDrive's South African safety page says a ride is insured from beginning to end, and its city-rides page says support submits a claim after an insured event. The public wording does not identify the insured parties, vehicle damage, liability limits, exclusions or excesses. inDrive Safety Pact inDrive South Africa city rides

Map cover across every stage

App offPrivate or declared commercial use
Online & waitingOften the least clearly documented stage
To pickupAccepted trip, no passenger yet
Passenger onboardPlatform benefit may apply, subject to terms

The safest exercise is simple: write down who covers vehicle damage, third-party property, passenger injury and the driver's own injury at each stage. Any blank cell is a question to resolve before the next trip.

What e-hailing insurance in South Africa should address

A robust arrangement starts with explicit e-hailing acceptance and then builds around the losses that would stop the car or the income. The exact sections, limits, excesses and conditions will vary by insurer.

It helps to understand what comprehensive car insurance normally sets out to protect, then identify the extra commercial-use conditions an e-hailing vehicle brings. Drivers using a company, rental or fleet structure should also review the broader commercial insurance context.

1

Own-vehicle damage

Accidental damage, fire, theft and hijacking while the vehicle is used as declared.

2

Third-party property

Damage the driver is legally liable to pay for after an insured event.

3

Passenger liability

Liability arising from injury to fare-paying passengers, with clear limits and exclusions.

4

Towing and assistance

Roadside support, towing destination, storage limits and after-hours contact.

5

Downtime options

Hire car, loss-of-use or defined income benefits, if offered and selected.

6

Finance shortfall

The potential gap between an insured settlement and the outstanding finance balance.

7

Accessories and security

Declared trackers, dashcams, panic devices and fitted accessories.

8

Driver structure

Every regular driver, owner, fleet, rental or vehicle-management arrangement.

Drivers comparing options can use Best Care's guide to compare policy wording, limits and excesses. A cheaper premium is not cheaper if the permitted use is wrong or a large excess makes the claim unaffordable.

Ask for written confirmation: “Does this policy cover my vehicle while I am logged into and working on Uber, Bolt and/or inDrive, including while waiting, travelling to collect a passenger and carrying the passenger?” Keep the reply with the schedule and wording.

Insurance sits beside operating-licence and PrDP compliance

Insurance does not make an unlicensed operation legal, and a licence does not create insurance cover. South African e-hailing drivers need to check both tracks.

The National Land Transport Amendment Act formally created e-hailing as a public-transport category. The final Second National Land Transport Regulations came into operation on 12 September 2025. They say e-hailing may be provided only where the platform is registered with the National Public Transport Regulator and an operating licence has been issued for the vehicle. Government Gazette 53335

The regulations gave holders of older licences 180 days to apply for conversion. A later Department of Transport notice confirmed that the clock ran from 12 September 2025. Because that transition period has passed, a driver relying on an older charter or metered-taxi licence should urgently confirm status with the relevant Provincial Regulatory Entity rather than assuming it remains sufficient. Department of Transport notice

Separately, official government guidance says anyone transporting passengers for income needs a Professional Driving Permit, or PrDP, in addition to an ordinary driving licence. It also lists a minimum age of 21 for a passenger-vehicle PrDP. South African Government PrDP guidance

Use the relevant PRE for current provincial procedures. Platform guides can help with forms, but Bolt itself warns that provincial requirements may vary. Compliance documents should be current, consistent with the vehicle and driver, and kept with proof of submission where the authority permits.

Your premium reflects how the vehicle actually works

There is no reliable universal percentage for what e-hailing cover “should” cost. Underwriters may consider kilometres, hours and times of operation, vehicle type and value, overnight parking, territory, tracking, claims history, driver experience, number of drivers, finance and fleet structure.

That detail is not paperwork for its own sake. The 2025 RTMC report recorded 11,485 road fatalities arising from 9,734 fatal crashes, with 35% of fatal crashes occurring between 17:00 and 22:00. Those are national road-safety figures, not e-hailing claim statistics, so they should not be used to calculate a driver's premium. They do, however, show why time and location can matter to risk assessment. RTMC State of Road Safety 2025

Give realistic estimates and update the insurer when the pattern changes. A weekend side income can become full-time use; a single-driver car can become a two-shift vehicle; and a new platform can change the declared exposure.

The claim gaps drivers discover too late

Most dangerous gaps begin with an assumption: that business use includes paid passengers, that an app protects the car, or that the named driver can quietly rotate with another driver.

The app is on, but no trip is accepted

A driver repositions while waiting for a request and crashes. Uber's public injury benefit begins only when a request is accepted. If the motor policy does not accept e-hailing activity during the waiting stage, there may be a gap. That is why stage-by-stage confirmation matters.

The vehicle is financed and written off

An insurer may settle on the insured-value basis in the policy while the finance balance is higher. If credit-shortfall cover was not selected, the owner can be left paying for a car that no longer exists.

Several drivers share one vehicle

The policy names one regular driver, but the car works two shifts with different people. If the real structure was not disclosed, the claim may turn into a dispute about material facts, rating and permitted drivers.

A passenger is injured

A platform benefit may pay defined injury benefits, but that is not necessarily the same as indemnifying the driver's legal liability. Passenger liability, platform injury cover and Road Accident Fund rights are separate questions that need fact-specific advice.

If a collision happens, follow safety and reporting steps first. Best Care's South African accident checklist and claims guidance can help organise evidence and notification, subject to the policy's own deadlines.

Take this disclosure list to your broker or insurer

A productive quotation starts with a complete description of the work. Gather the following before asking for terms:

  • Every platform used, including Uber, Bolt, inDrive or a smaller service.
  • Full-time, part-time, weekend or seasonal use.
  • Estimated kilometres, hours, trip volume, operating areas and night work.
  • The registered owner, finance provider and any rental or fleet agreement.
  • Every regular or relief driver and their licence, PrDP and claims history.
  • Overnight parking, tracker, immobiliser, dashcam, panic device and other modifications.
  • Desired sections for own damage, third-party property, passenger liability, downtime and credit shortfall.

If the risk needs a commercial route, review the basics of commercial vehicle and fleet insurance rather than forcing it into a private-use product. If the same vehicle still has personal use, make sure both uses are recorded.

Key takeaways

  • Declare passenger-for-reward use and obtain written acceptance for every platform you drive on.
  • “Comprehensive” motor insurance does not automatically mean e-hailing use is permitted.
  • Platform protection may cover defined people or trip events without covering damage to the driver's car.
  • Map cover across app-off, waiting, pickup and passenger-onboard stages.
  • Keep the PrDP, vehicle operating licence and platform requirements separate from insurance.
  • Disclose all drivers, kilometres, territories, parking, security, finance and fleet arrangements.

Frequently asked questions

Does normal comprehensive car insurance cover Uber or Bolt driving?

Not automatically. Comprehensive describes the range of insured events, not the permitted use of the car. The insurer must know that you carry passengers for reward, and the schedule or wording must expressly accept that e-hailing use.

Is Uber's Partner Injury Protection enough for a driver?

No. Uber states that Partner Injury Protection is accident insurance for people while On-Trip and is not commercial vehicle insurance or a substitute for comprehensive motor cover.

Does Bolt insure a driver's car in South Africa?

Do not assume so. We could not locate a current public South African Bolt motor policy wording that promises comprehensive damage cover for a driver's vehicle. Ask Bolt support for the current document and arrange your own disclosed e-hailing motor cover.

Are inDrive rides insured in South Africa?

inDrive's South African site says rides are insured from beginning to end, but its public page does not specify the insured parties, vehicle-damage cover, limits or excesses. Treat that statement as platform protection, not proof that your own car is comprehensively insured.

Do e-hailing drivers need a PrDP in South Africa?

Yes. South African government guidance says a driver transporting passengers for income needs a Professional Driving Permit in addition to an ordinary driving licence.

Do e-hailing drivers need an operating licence?

Yes. Under the final regulations effective from 12 September 2025, e-hailing may be provided only through a registered platform and with an operating licence issued for the vehicle.

What should I disclose when asking for e-hailing insurance?

Disclose every platform used, full-time or part-time use, estimated kilometres and hours, operating areas and times, all regular drivers, ownership or finance details, overnight parking, security devices, modifications and previous claims.

What happens if I do not disclose e-hailing use?

A claim may be rejected or the policy may be cancelled if the actual commercial use falls outside the agreed use or a material fact was not disclosed. The exact outcome depends on the policy, facts and applicable law, so obtain the insurer's acceptance in writing before driving.

The right question is not “am I insured?”

The useful question is: “Which policy responds to which loss, at which trip stage, for which driver?” Answer that in writing and the gaps become visible.

Start with honest disclosure, legal documents and the vehicle's real working pattern. Then compare cover, excesses, limits and conditions, not just the monthly premium. A short-term insurance broker can help turn those facts into a clearer quotation brief.
